growth_story.headline: Growth of 4.4 percent a year from 2004 to 2013 gave way to a collapse that left Venezuela's income per person 70.4 percent below its 1977 peak.
growth_story.arc: Venezuela's income per person peaked in 1977 and is now 70.4 percent below that peak, lower than in 1960, the first year of the record. From 1990 to 2003 it shrank by 1.0 percent a year, ending with falls of 10.4 percent in 2002 and 9.4 percent in 2003, around an oil strike that began in December 2002. From 2004 to 2013 it grew by 4.4 percent a year, while the state took near-full control of the oil sector and its income. From 2014 to 2025 it shrank by 8.1 percent a year: the fall in oil prices from mid-2014 magnified long-running problems in oil production, oil export income collapsed and price controls crippled other domestic production, and income per person fell 25.4 percent in 2019 and 28.6 percent in 2020. Growth has been positive every year since 2021, reaching 8.2 percent in 2022 before slowing to 1.2 percent in 2025, while the IMF still describes a deep economic, political and humanitarian crisis that has driven a large share of the population abroad.

growth_story.tension: The data show income per person growing every year from 2021 to 2025, but in October 2025 the IMF described mounting challenges and a deep crisis, and said its figures for recent years are mostly staff estimates to be read with caution ("For most indicators, data for 2018–24 are IMF staff estimates."). With a large share of the population gone abroad since 2014, some of the measured gain in income per person may reflect fewer people rather than more output.
